questions.question: Compare high-, middle- and low-income residential areas in South African cities.
questions.expected_answer: High-income areas have large houses on big plots of about a thousand square metres or more, with gardens, pools, garages and often walls and security, low housing density, curved quiet tree-lined streets, private schools and parks nearby, are often on the edges of cities or on high ground away from industry, and residents mostly use cars; examples include Sandton, Waterkloof and Constantia. Middle-income areas have medium houses on smaller plots, townhouses and flats, higher density, often grid streets, with schools, clinics, shops and sports fields within reach and a mix of car and public transport use. Low-income areas have the highest density: apartheid-era townships such as Soweto, Umlazi, Mdantsane and Khayelitsha, hostels, RDP houses of at least 40 square metres, backyard rooms and informal settlements of self-built shelters without formal services, with shared taps and toilets; they are often far from the CBD and jobs, so residents spend much time and money on taxis, buses and trains.

questions.question: Explain how segregation and apartheid shaped residential areas in South African cities.
questions.expected_answer: Segregation laws such as the Natives (Urban Areas) Act of 1923 placed African people in separate locations on the edges of towns. The Group Areas Act of 1950 divided every city into areas for white, coloured, Indian and African people and forced people out of areas declared for other groups, as in District Six, Sophiatown and Cato Manor; about three and a half million people were moved in forced removals of all kinds between 1960 and 1983. The apartheid city placed white suburbs near the CBD on the best land with good services, coloured and Indian areas further out, and African townships furthest out, separated by buffer zones and under-served because Africans were treated as temporary residents, with pass laws controlling entry. After 1994 these laws ended and some families moved into former white suburbs, but high land prices and new housing on cheap distant land kept poor households on the edges; cities now promote mixed-income housing near transport and jobs, such as Cosmo City, and upgrade settlements in place.

questions.question: Describe the hierarchy of shopping centres and the location of services and recreation areas in a city.
questions.expected_answer: Corner shops, spaza shops and street traders sell low-order goods such as bread, milk and airtime close to home; neighbourhood centres have a supermarket, pharmacy and small shops; regional malls such as Canal Walk, Gateway and the Mall of Africa sell high-order goods, have department stores, cinemas and car parks, and are located at highway and main road junctions; township malls such as Maponya Mall, opened in 2007, now serve townships. Services also form a hierarchy: primary schools, clinics and police stations serve local areas, high schools, hospitals and courts serve larger areas, and universities and specialist hospitals such as Chris Hani Baragwanath serve the city or province; townships were deliberately under-served under apartheid. Recreation areas include parks, sports fields, stadiums, golf courses, beaches and reserves, from local parks to city-wide sites such as FNB Stadium, the Durban beachfront and Table Mountain National Park, and are often on land unsuitable for building such as flood plains, steep slopes and wetlands; wealthier areas have more green space per person.
